summary:
The score h is the largest number such that h papers each have at least h citations. Sorting the papers by
citations (most first) makes it a simple scan: the score is the last position i where the i-th paper has at
least i citations. Since h can never exceed n, counting papers per citation level (capped at n) avoids the
sort and gives O(n).

question.md:
Return the largest h such that **at least h** papers have **at least h** citations each.

- **Both conditions use the same h.** With `[3, 0, 6, 1, 5]`, three papers have ≥ 3 citations, so h ≥ 3;
  only two have ≥ 4, so h = 3.
- **h ≤ n:** you can't have more than n papers. A huge citation count doesn't raise h past the number of
  papers.
- **h can be 0** (no paper has any citation, or `[0]`).
- **Size:** up to 10⁵ papers; citations up to 10⁹.

think.md:
Take `[3, 0, 6, 1, 5, 4, 8]`. Sort them, most cited first: `[8, 6, 5, 4, 3, 1, 0]`. Read along: the 1st paper has 8 ≥ 1,
the 2nd has 6 ≥ 2, the 3rd has 5 ≥ 3, the 4th has 4 ≥ 4, the 5th has 3 < 5. So 4 papers have at least 4
citations, and 5 papers don't have 5 each: h = 4.

think.caption: The first 4 papers (most cited) each have at least 4 citations.

think.md:
Counting view: "how many papers have ≥ h citations?" only goes **down** as h goes up, while the requirement
h goes up. The answer is where they cross. Since h ≤ n, any citation count above n can be treated as n,
which lets us count papers per level in an array of size n + 1 instead of sorting.

approaches.title: Try every h

idea.md: For h = n, n − 1, …, 0: count the papers with at least h citations. The first h whose count is ≥ h is the answer.

build: For h from n down to 0: count papers with `citations ≥ h`.
Return the first h with `count ≥ h`.

lines.text: From the largest possible score downwards, so the first success is the maximum.
How many papers reach h citations? Enough of them means h works.

walk.title: Try h from n down to 0; count papers with at least h citations; the first h that works is the answer.

limits.md: Each h recounts all papers. Sorting once answers every "how many have ≥ h?" by position.

approaches.title: Sort descending and scan

idea.md: Sort citations from most to least. The i-th paper (1-based) is the weakest of the top i. While it has at least i citations, the top i papers all have ≥ i, so h is at least i. The first failure ends the scan.

build: For i = 1, 2, …: if `s[i − 1] ≥ i`, set `h = i`; otherwise stop.

notes.java: Java sorts `int[]` ascending, so the scan reads it from the end.
notes.cpp: Sorting with reverse iterators gives descending order.
notes.c: A comparator with the arguments swapped sorts descending.

lines.text: `h` papers are confirmed; the next one (the (h + 1)-th most cited) must have at least h + 1 citations to raise the score.

complexity.md: **Time O(n log n).** **Space O(n)** for the copy.

steps.text: Paper #1 has 8 ≥ 1 citations, so 1 papers have at least 1 each.
Paper #2 has 6 ≥ 2 citations, so 2 papers have at least 2 each.
Paper #3 has 5 ≥ 3 citations, so 3 papers have at least 3 each.
Paper #4 has 4 ≥ 4 citations, so 4 papers have at least 4 each.
Paper #5 has only 3 < 5: stop. The score is 4.

walk.title: Sort descending. The i-th paper (1-based) has at least i citations as long as citations[i − 1] ≥ i.

limits.md: We sort values up to 10⁹, but only whether each count is ≥ some h ≤ n matters. Capping at n and counting replaces the sort.

approaches.title: Count papers per citation level

idea.md: `bucket[c]` = number of papers with exactly c citations, where any count above n is put in `bucket[n]`. Walk h from n down, accumulating `bucket[h]` into "papers with ≥ h". The first h where that total reaches h is the answer.

build: `bucket` of size n + 1; add each paper to `bucket[min(c, n)]`.
`atLeast = 0`; for h from n down to 0: `atLeast += bucket[h]`; if `atLeast ≥ h`, return h.

lines.text: Papers per citation level. Levels above n can't make h larger than n, so they're merged into level n; this keeps the array at n + 1 slots.
From high to low, `atLeast` = papers with at least h citations. It only grows as h shrinks; the first h it reaches is the largest that works.
h = 0 always works, so the loop always returns.

notes.c: Free the buckets and return the h where the loop stopped.

steps.text: bucket[c] = papers with exactly c citations; anything above 7 goes into bucket 7.
h = 4: papers with ≥ 4 citations = 4 ≥ h → answer.

walk.title: The score is at most n = 7. Count papers per citation level (capping at n), then walk down accumulating.

takeaways.md:
- "Largest h such that at least h items are ≥ h" is answered by sorting descending and scanning, or by
  **counting sort with values capped at n**.
- When the answer is bounded by n, values larger than n can be clamped, which makes counting feasible.
